---
title: "Getting started with ezrsurvey"
jupyter: python3
---

`ezrsurvey` turns the things consumer-survey analysts do over and over into
single-line helpers. This article walks through a typical analysis of the
bundled `podracing_survey` dataset: from raw answers to percentages, models,
diagnostics and a chart you could drop on a slide.

```{python}
import ezrsurvey as ez
```

## The data

`podracing_survey` is 1,000 simulated respondents with demographics, a 0 to 10
NPS question, worded feature ratings, multi-select motivations, brand questions
and open-text comments.

```{python}
ez.podracing_survey[["respondent_id", "demo_gender", "demo_age", "nps_value"]]
```

## Percentages without the groupby, count and pivot dance

`calc_percentage()` is the workhorse: counts, percentages and ordering in one
call. Columns are named as strings.

```{python}
ez.calc_percentage(ez.podracing_survey, "demo_gender", sort="desc")
```

Group with `by`, and pivot to a wide cross-tab with `wide=True`:

```{python}
ez.calc_percentage(ez.podracing_survey, "satis_return", by="region", wide=True)
```

Check-all-that-apply questions live in a block of columns sharing a prefix;
`calc_percentage_multi()` handles the per-respondent denominator for you:

```{python}
ez.calc_percentage_multi(ez.podracing_survey, "motivations_", id="respondent_id", sort="desc")
```

Spreadsheet exports, Google Forms among them, instead pack every answer a
respondent ticked into a single cell. The same function recognises that shape
and separates the answers, so you do not have to reshape anything first:

```{python}
import pandas as pd

packed = pd.DataFrame({
    "respondent": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    "motivations": ["Speed; Drivers", "Speed", "", "Betting; Speed"],
})

ez.calc_percentage_multi(packed, "motivations", id="respondent", sort="desc")
```

Note the denominator: three respondents ticked something, so "Speed" is 3 of 3.
When you need those answers as columns rather than as a table, for a crosstab or
a filter, `split_multi()` widens them:

```{python}
ez.split_multi(packed, "motivations")
```

## Reusable level orders

Rather than retyping `levels=[...]`, register an order once and link it to a
variable; `calc_percentage()` then applies it automatically.

```{python}
ez.register_order(
    "education",
    levels=[
        "Primary or less",
        "Lower secondary",
        "Upper secondary",
        "Short-cycle tertiary",
        "Bachelor or equivalent",
        "Master or equivalent",
        "Doctoral or equivalent",
    ],
    vars="demo_edu",
)

ez.calc_percentage(ez.podracing_survey, "demo_edu")
```

## Net Promoter Score

```{python}
ez.calc_nps(ez.podracing_survey, "nps_value")
```

```{python}
ez.plot_nps(ez.podracing_survey, "nps_value")
```

## Importance / performance

`ipm_model()` combines driver importance (by default, relative weights against
the NPS score) with feature performance; `plot_ipm()` draws the matrix. Pass
`method="forest"` for a random-forest cross-check, which sees non-linear effects
that relative weights cannot. The forest needs the `drivers` extra
(`pip install "ezrsurvey[drivers]"`).

```{python}
model = ez.ipm_model(ez.podracing_survey, "nps_value", "ratings_")
model
```

## Comparing two events

For event surveys you often compare this wave with the last. `compare_values()`
computes the differences and `plot_diff()` draws the change chart.

```{python}
previous = model.copy()
previous["performance"] = model["performance"] - [0.3, -0.1, 0.2, 0, 0.1, 0.3]

ez.plot_diff(ez.compare_values(model, previous))
```

## How precise is it?

`diagnose()` reports the standard error, relative standard error and margin of
error for any column: numeric (a point estimate) or categorical (a proportion).

```{python}
ez.diagnose(ez.podracing_survey, "demo_gender", "nps_value")
```

For a one-shot, plain-language read on the whole study, `precision_summary()`
picks the point-scale and proportion variables for you and writes the bullet
points you would otherwise hand-craft for a report appendix:

```{python}
ez.precision_summary(ez.podracing_survey)
```

### Why relative standard error?

A standard error on its own is hard to judge: is plus or minus 0.05 good? It
depends on the scale. The **relative standard error** (RSE) divides the standard
error by the estimate, so precision becomes comparable across a 1 to 5 rating
and a percentage alike. Rating estimates by their RSE is the approach national
statistical agencies use to decide whether a number is solid enough to publish.
The [Australian Bureau of
Statistics](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/microdata-tablebuilder/tablebuilder/confidentiality-and-relative-standard-error),
for example, treats an RSE of 25% or more as not reliable for most purposes,
marks estimates between 25% and 50% with an asterisk as ones to use with
caution, and suppresses anything above 50%. ezrsurvey keeps that 25% boundary
and adds tighter bands below it, because in consumer-survey work the question is
usually which of several adequately precise numbers to lead with:

| RSE | Rating |
|---|---|
| under 5% | high precision |
| under 10% | precise |
| under 15% | satisfactory |
| under 25% | use with caution |
| 25% or more | likely reliability issues |

For proportions, the margin of error is widest at a 50/50 split
(`sqrt(0.5 * 0.5 / n)`), so a single worst-case percentage-point figure at your
achieved sample size bounds every percentage in the study, which is why
`precision_summary()` reports it.

## Saving and exporting

Every table and chart has a one-line save. A bare file name lands in an
`ezrsurvey-outputs/` folder, created on demand, so a script's results collect in
one place instead of scattering through the working directory; pass a path with
a directory in it (`"./gender.xlsx"`, `"tables/gender.xlsx"`, anything absolute)
to put a file exactly where you want it. The first save of a session says which
folder it used, so nothing goes missing. Excel files need the `excel` extra.

```python
ez.save_data(ez.calc_percentage(ez.podracing_survey, "demo_gender"), "gender.xlsx")
ez.save_plot(ez.plot_nps(ez.podracing_survey, "nps_value"), "nps.png")

# several tables, one tab each
ez.export_xlsx(
    gender=ez.calc_percentage(ez.podracing_survey, "demo_gender"),
    job=ez.calc_percentage(ez.podracing_survey, "demo_job"),
    path="summary.xlsx",
)
```

Every helper also takes the data frame first, so a pandas method chain works
with `.pipe()`:

```{python}
ez.podracing_survey.pipe(ez.calc_percentage, "demo_job", sort="desc")
```

  (`use_ezrsurvey_profile()`).
* Build a deck with `report_deck()` or scaffold a Quarto report with
  `scaffold_report()`, which drops the `.qmd` beside where its render will land.

```{python}
#| include: false
ez.remove_order("education")
```
